3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

Free cash flow

Section titled “Free cash flow”

3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models valued stocks with dividends, but for many companies dividends have little to do with the cash the company generates. Another approach is to estimate first the cash the operating business generates, and then divide it between shareholders and creditors.

The cash from operations left after the investment needed to maintain and expand the business, available to all investors (shareholders and creditors), is free cash flow to the firm (FCFF):

FCFF=EBIT(1−t)+Dep−CapEx−ΔWC\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT}(1 - t) + \text{Dep} - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{WC}FCFF=EBIT(1−t)+Dep−CapEx−ΔWC

EBIT(1−t)\text{EBIT}(1 - t)EBIT(1−t) is after-tax operating profit as if the company had no debt (NOPAT), Dep is depreciation, CapEx is capital spending, and ΔWC\Delta \text{WC}ΔWC is the increase in working capital (3.7 Financial Statement Analysis). FCFF does not deduct interest: it measures the cash of the business itself, whatever the financing.

The cash that belongs to shareholders alone is free cash flow to equity (FCFE). From FCFF, subtract after-tax interest paid to creditors and add net borrowing ΔD\Delta DΔD (new borrowing minus repayments):

FCFE=FCFF−Int(1−t)+ΔD\text{FCFE} = \text{FCFF} - \text{Int}(1 - t) + \Delta DFCFE=FCFF−Int(1−t)+ΔD
Check C1
Why is interest expense not deducted when computing free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)?
Interest is cash the company actually pays.
Interest is tax-deductible, which is reflected in the after-tax cost of debt, but that is not why FCFF leaves interest out.
Interest can be large; the reason it is left out has nothing to do with its size.

The weighted average cost of capital

Section titled “The weighted average cost of capital”

FCFF belongs to shareholders and creditors, so it is discounted at a weighted average of the returns both require. Let EEE and DDD be the market values of equity and debt, V=D+EV = D + EV=D+E, rEr_ErE​ the cost of equity (cost of equity), rDr_DrD​ the interest rate on debt, and ttt the tax rate:

WACC=EVrE+DVrD(1−t)\text{WACC} = \frac{E}{V} r_E + \frac{D}{V} r_D (1 - t)WACC=VE​rE​+VD​rD​(1−t)

This is the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). The cost of debt is multiplied by 1−t1 - t1−t because interest is deducted before tax: for each dollar of interest, the company pays ttt dollars less tax. This tax saving is the interest tax shield. FCFF computes taxes as if there were no debt, so the benefit of the tax shield goes into the discount rate.

The weights use market values, not book values: the returns investors require apply to the amounts they put in (or could take out) today.

Check C2
Other things equal, when the corporate tax rate falls, the WACC of a company with debt rises slightly.
Think: how does the cost of debt enter the WACC? What role does the tax rate play in it?

Steps of a DCF valuation

Section titled “Steps of a DCF valuation”

A valuation with FCFF usually takes several steps:

  1. Forecast FCFF for the next TTT years (often 5 to 10): revenue growth, margins, capital spending and working capital, ideally checked against the ratios of 3.8 Financial Ratios and the industry.
  2. Estimate the value after the forecast period, the terminal value. A common method assumes growth at a rate ggg that can last forever: TVT=FCFFT+1WACC−g\text{TV}_T = \frac{\text{FCFF}_{T+1}}{\text{WACC} - g}TVT​=WACC−gFCFFT+1​​.
  3. Discount each year’s FCFF and the terminal value to today at the WACC, to get the enterprise value:
EV=∑t=1TFCFFt(1+WACC)t+TVT(1+WACC)T\text{EV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\text{FCFF}_t}{(1 + \text{WACC})^t} + \frac{\text{TV}_T}{(1 + \text{WACC})^T}EV=t=1∑T​(1+WACC)tFCFFt​​+(1+WACC)TTVT​​
  1. Enterprise value belongs to all investors. Subtract net debt (interest-bearing debt minus cash) to get equity value, and divide by the number of shares to get value per share.

One can also discount FCFE at the cost of equity rEr_ErE​ to get equity value directly. With consistent assumptions, the two methods should give the same result.

Growth and value

Section titled “Growth and value”

Growth needs investment. Let NOPAT1\text{NOPAT}_1NOPAT1​ be next year’s NOPAT, ROIC (return on invested capital) the return on new investment, and ggg the growth rate. One can show (Exercises Question 4) that, if all of these stay constant,

EV=NOPAT1(1−gROIC)WACC−g\text{EV} = \frac{\text{NOPAT}_1 \left(1 - \frac{g}{\text{ROIC}}\right)}{\text{WACC} - g}EV=WACC−gNOPAT1​(1−ROICg​)​

gROIC\frac{g}{\text{ROIC}}ROICg​ is the share of profit that must be reinvested to grow at ggg. Growth makes the denominator smaller, but also the numerator: the faster the growth, the more money must be invested, and the less cash goes to investors.

Check C3
In Figure 4-1, set the ROIC on new investment to 6% and the WACC to 8%, then raise the growth rate. Firm value:
Growth needs reinvestment. New investment earns 6% while investors require 8%; does each new investment create positive or negative value?
Growth leaves value unchanged only if new investment earns exactly the WACC. Are they equal here?
Raise growth from 0 step by step in the figure and see whether the multiple first rises and then falls.

Common mistakes

Section titled “Common mistakes”

A DCF has a clear structure, but the result depends entirely on the inputs. Common mistakes include:

  • The terminal value is most of the value (often more than half), and small changes in long-run growth and the WACC change it a lot. Long-run growth should not exceed the economy’s long-run nominal growth and must be below the WACC.
  • Growth and reinvestment are inconsistent: forecasting high growth without the capital spending and working capital it requires.
  • Cash flows and discount rates are inconsistent: FCFF must be discounted at the WACC and FCFE at the cost of equity; nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates (real interest rate).
  • Double counting or omissions: forgetting to subtract debt when going from enterprise value to equity value, or adding an item that is already in the cash flows.

So a DCF usually comes with a sensitivity analysis: a table of values for different WACCs and long-run growth rates, to see whether the conclusion depends on one particular assumption.

Check C4
A company has negative FCFF in every year of a 5-year forecast period (it is investing heavily). Its DCF enterprise value must also be negative.
Think: besides the cash flows in the forecast period, what else does enterprise value include? What might heavy investment bring later?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • FCFF=EBIT(1−t)+Dep−CapEx−ΔWC\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT}(1 - t) + \text{Dep} - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{WC}FCFF=EBIT(1−t)+Dep−CapEx−ΔWC belongs to all investors; FCFE=FCFF−Int(1−t)+ΔD\text{FCFE} = \text{FCFF} - \text{Int}(1 - t) + \Delta DFCFE=FCFF−Int(1−t)+ΔD belongs to shareholders.
  • WACC=EVrE+DVrD(1−t)\text{WACC} = \frac{E}{V} r_E + \frac{D}{V} r_D (1 - t)WACC=VE​rE​+VD​rD​(1−t), weighted by market values; the interest tax shield enters through the after-tax cost of debt.
  • DCF: FCFF over the forecast period plus the terminal value, discounted at the WACC, gives enterprise value; subtracting net debt gives equity value.
  • EV=NOPAT1(1−gROIC)WACC−g\text{EV} = \frac{\text{NOPAT}_1 \left(1 - \frac{g}{\text{ROIC}}\right)}{\text{WACC} - g}EV=WACC−gNOPAT1​(1−ROICg​)​: growth needs reinvestment.
  • The terminal value is a large share, so results are very sensitive to long-run growth and the WACC; cash flows and discount rates must be consistent.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
A company's FCFF over the next 3 years is expected to be 100, 110 and 120, growing 3% a year forever after. The WACC is 8%, net debt 500, and there are 100 shares.
(a) Find enterprise value and value per share. What percentage of enterprise value is the present value of the terminal value?
(b) If long-run growth were 4%, how would value per share change (qualitatively)? What does this suggest about using DCF results?
Question 2
A company's FCFF this year is 100, interest expense 20, tax rate 25%; this year it borrowed 30 and repaid 20.
(a) What is FCFE?
(b) A company keeps FCFE above FCFF every year by borrowing more and more. When valuing it with FCFE, can this go on forever? How should borrowing be treated in the valuation?
Question 3
A company is considering more debt. Debt is now 20% of capital (at market value), the cost of equity 9% and the interest rate 4%. If debt rises to 50%, the cost of equity will rise to 12% and the interest rate to 5.2%. The tax rate is 25%.
(a) What is the WACC under each capital structure?
(b) Why does the WACC change little, or even rise, when the debt ratio rises so much?
